youtube.aciklama:
How much ambient noise is acceptable in an audiometric test room? In this lesson we cover the MPANL concept, the ANSI S3.1 and ISO 8253-1 limits, the different values for supra-aural earphones, insert earphones and ears not covered, and how to measure noise in octave bands.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: ANSI/ASA S3.1-1999 (R2018), Maximum Permissible Ambient Noise Levels for Audiometric Test Rooms; ISO 8253-1, Acoustics: Audiometric test methods, Part 1; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Gelfand, Essentials of Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn the maximum permissible ambient noise levels in a test room and how they are measured.
Step by step, we will look at the limits in the ANSI and ISO standards, how they vary by earphone type, and octave band measurement.
In earlier lessons we saw how calibration ensures the audiometer produces the right sound, but the right sound only counts in a quiet room.
Ambient noise is the unwanted background sound present in the room during testing.
This noise partly masks the test tone and makes the person's threshold look worse than it is.
The people most affected are those with normal hearing, whose thresholds are around zero decibels HL.
This is because their thresholds are closest to the level where the masking effect of the noise begins.
So the standards define in numbers which noise level must not be exceeded in a test room.
The sources of noise in a test room are often everyday sounds that are hard to notice.
First come ventilation and air conditioning systems; their hum is steady and mostly low-pitched.
Fans in the control room computer and equipment also create a low but constant noise.
Footsteps in the corridor, the elevator, doors and outside traffic are carried into the room through the building.
Conversations in the waiting room or control room can leak into the booth if the door does not close well.
Buzzing from some lamps and vibrating surfaces also make small but measurable contributions.

maddeler.metin: For testing down to 0 dB HL

cumleler: Our key concept is the maximum permissible ambient noise level, or MPANL.
MPANL is the highest noise level that can be present in the room during testing without meaningfully changing threshold.
The values are not a single number; they are split into frequency bands and given as octave or third-octave band levels.
The tables assume that thresholds can be measured down to zero decibels HL.
The ANSI limits are the levels at which ambient noise masks the test tone by no more than about two decibels.
So in a room below the limits, the effect of noise on threshold stays well below our five decibel test step.
The limits depend on the test condition, because the noise reaching the ear depends on what covers the ear.
The cushion of a supra-aural earphone reduces outside noise somewhat.
This reduction is weak at low frequencies and more marked at high frequencies.
The foam tip of an insert earphone seals the ear canal, so it blocks outside noise much better, especially at low frequencies.
In bone conduction and sound field testing, the ears are uncovered, and noise reaches the ear without any reduction.
That is why the strictest limits apply to the ears not covered condition.
This graph shows the ANSI S3.1 octave band limits for testing from one hundred twenty five to eight thousand hertz.
The horizontal axis shows octave band center frequencies, and the vertical axis the permissible level in decibels SPL.
The blue line at the top is for testing with insert earphones; here the permissible noise is highest.
The navy line in the middle is for supra-aural earphones; in the low bands the limit drops clearly.
The red line at the bottom is for ears not covered; from one to four kilohertz the limit is eleven to fourteen decibels SPL.
With ears not covered, the limit is lowest in the mid and high frequency region where our ears are most sensitive.
The difference between the two earphones is greatest in the two hundred fifty and five hundred hertz bands, in the low region.
Let us see the same values as a table; all values are octave band levels in decibels SPL.
In the one hundred twenty five hertz band, the limit is thirty five for supra-aural, fifty nine for insert, and twenty nine uncovered.
In the two hundred fifty hertz band, these values are twenty five, fifty three and twenty one decibels.
In the five hundred hertz band, the limits are twenty one, fifty and sixteen decibels.
In the one kilohertz band, the limit is twenty six for supra-aural earphones and only thirteen decibels for ears not covered.
In the two, four and eight kilohertz bands, the limit for ears not covered stays between eleven and fourteen decibels.
These values are for testing down to zero decibels HL, starting from one hundred twenty five hertz.
If testing starts at five hundred hertz, the standard allows higher levels in the one hundred twenty five and two hundred fifty hertz bands.
ANSI S3.1 is the standard used in the United States; it gives limits in octave and third-octave bands.
It has tables for three ranges, for testing that starts at one hundred twenty five, two hundred fifty or five hundred hertz.
ISO 8253-1 is the international standard that defines the method of pure tone audiometry; it also sets limits for the test environment.
In the ISO approach, the aim is that ambient noise adds no more than plus two decibels of uncertainty at zero decibels HL.
The tables of the two standards are not identical; the measurement report should state which standard was used.
The measurement uses a high-accuracy class sound level meter with octave or third-octave filters.
The meter itself is checked with an acoustic calibrator before the measurement.
The microphone is placed where the patient's head will be during testing, at ear height.
The measurement should reflect real test conditions: door closed, with ventilation, lights and computers running.
Then the level of each octave band from one hundred twenty five hertz to eight kilohertz is read separately.
Each band value is compared with the limit for the test condition used, and results are recorded with the date and equipment details.
Now let us examine the results from an entirely hypothetical test room.
The gray bars show the noise level measured in each octave band; the energy is concentrated in the low bands.
The navy line is the supra-aural limit; in the bands from one kilohertz up, the measured values are clearly below it.
But in the one hundred twenty five, two hundred fifty and five hundred hertz bands, the measured noise exceeds the limit.
The dashed blue line is the insert earphone limit; the same room is acceptable for insert earphones in all bands.
For bone conduction testing with ears uncovered, though, this room fails in many bands; those limits are much lower.
A single A-weighted decibel value is not enough for this assessment, because the limits are set separately for each band.
Noise can change during the day; repeating the measurement during the clinic's busiest hours gives a realistic picture.
It is usually repeated with the yearly checks and after any change, such as new ventilation, construction or a move.
The tables are for testing down to zero decibels HL; if screening only at higher levels, the limits can be raised by the same amount.
When the limit is exceeded, first find the source; it is often a fan, a ventilation outlet or a door that does not close well.
Turning the ventilation down during testing or moving equipment away from the booth sometimes solves the problem on its own.
For earphone testing, using insert earphones greatly reduces the effect of noise in the low bands.
For a lasting fix, door seals are replaced, the booth is moved to a quieter place, or a double-walled booth is installed.
If testing goes on before the fix, the report clearly states the test condition and the frequencies that may be affected.
The trace of ambient noise on the audiogram forms a recognizable pattern.
Here, a person with normal hearing has unexpectedly poor thresholds at two fifty and five hundred hertz compared with high frequencies.
Bone conduction is measured with ears uncovered, so it is affected more; this can make the air-bone gap look smaller than it is.
If the same person's thresholds are inconsistent at different times of day, ambient noise should come to mind.
When you see such a pattern, first check the room noise and the placement of the earphones.

sahneler.metin: If low-frequency thresholds are unexpectedly poor, repeat the test with insert earphones; if thresholds improve, have the booth noise measured.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: even without a sound level meter, you can do a simple check.
Measure the thresholds of a colleague with normal hearing, first with supra-aural earphones, then with insert earphones.
If low-frequency thresholds improve clearly with insert earphones, low-pitched noise in the room may be exceeding the limit.
This simple observation does not replace measurement, but it shows when an octave band measurement is needed.

maddeler.metin: MPANL: the _highest_ noise that spares threshold
Measured in octave bands, at head position

cumleler: MPANL is the highest ambient noise level that does not meaningfully change thresholds at zero decibels HL.
Insert earphones allow the widest tolerance and supra-aural earphones a narrower one; the difference is greatest in the low bands.
In bone conduction and sound field testing the ears are uncovered, so the limits are lowest.
Noise is measured with a precision sound level meter, in octave bands, at the patient's head position, and the result is recorded.

sahneler.soru: Under which condition are the limits strictest?
sahneler.aciklama: With ears uncovered, noise reaches the ear _without any reduction_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: under which test condition are the permissible ambient noise limits lowest?

cumleler: The correct answer is C: the ears not covered condition.
In bone conduction and sound field testing no earphone covers the ear, so the same noise spoils threshold much more easily.
